tasks.title: Compare Average Wait Time by Unit
tasks.context: Hospital operations leadership wants an aggregate comparison of waiting time across service units. The dataset contains unit-day totals only and no patient identifiers.
tasks.goal: Calculate average waiting time at the correct unit grain.
tasks.deliverable: Return unit and avg_wait_minutes rounded to one decimal.
tasks.prompt: Query hospital_daily_ops. Return unit and ROUND(AVG(avg_wait_minutes), 1) AS avg_wait_minutes, grouped by unit.
hints: Each row is one unit-day, not one patient.
Use AVG(avg_wait_minutes).
GROUP BY unit and round to one decimal.
tasks.explanation: This gives an aggregate operational comparison. It does not measure clinical severity or quality of treatment.

tasks.title: Validate the Operations Extract
tasks.context: Before a capacity meeting, you receive an aggregate unit-day operations extract.
tasks.goal: Identify the required validation checks without inventing patient-level data.
tasks.prompt: Which checks should be completed before analysis?
expectedSelections: Check that each unit-date combination is unique.
Validate non-negative counts and waiting times.
Check that completed visits do not exceed arrivals.
Treat zero staffed beds as not-applicable for non-bed outpatient capacity unless documentation says otherwise.
hints: Start with grain and uniqueness.
Then check impossible numeric relationships.
A zero can mean not-applicable, not necessarily missing.
tasks.explanation: Operational data quality starts with grain, domain constraints, and documented meaning. Do not fabricate missing patient-level values.
options: Check that each unit-date combination is unique.
Validate non-negative counts and waiting times.
Check that completed visits do not exceed arrivals.
Treat zero staffed beds as not-applicable for non-bed outpatient capacity unless documentation says otherwise.
Create synthetic patient names for every row.
Replace every unusual value with the overall average without investigation.

tasks.title: Interpret an Average Wait-Time Increase
tasks.context: Emergency average wait time rose on two days. Leadership asks whether the experience worsened for everyone.
tasks.expectedAnswer: The average suggests an operational signal, but inspect the wait-time distribution or percentiles and volume mix before claiming every visit experienced a longer wait
hints: A mean can move because of a tail.
Volume mix can change the aggregate.
Operational conclusions should distinguish a signal from a universal claim.
tasks.explanation: Means can hide skew and subgroup changes. A good analyst requests distributional evidence before making a broad statement.
options: The average suggests an operational signal, but inspect the wait-time distribution or percentiles and volume mix before claiming every visit experienced a longer wait
Every visit definitely waited longer
Average wait time is never useful
The result proves a clinical treatment problem

tasks.title: Find Forecast Capacity Gaps
tasks.context: The operations team has a day-of-week arrival forecast and planned service capacity.
tasks.goal: Identify days where expected demand exceeds planned capacity.
tasks.deliverable: Return day_name and capacity_gap for positive gaps only.
tasks.prompt: Query hospital_capacity_forecast. Return day_name and expected_arrivals - planned_capacity AS capacity_gap where expected arrivals exceed planned capacity.
hints: The gap is demand minus planned capacity.
Filter to rows where expected_arrivals > planned_capacity.
No GROUP BY is required because the table is already one row per day name.
tasks.explanation: The query identifies operational planning pressure. A gap is not a clinical recommendation; it is an input to staffing and scheduling review.

tasks.title: Choose a Demand Forecasting Approach
tasks.context: Saturday demand is repeatedly higher than early-week demand. The manager asks for next month’s staffing input.
tasks.prompt: Which approach is strongest for a first operational forecast?
tasks.expectedAnswer: Model day-of-week seasonality using several comparable weeks, validate forecast error, and add scenario ranges before staffing decisions
hints: One busy day should not define the future.
Repeated day-of-week patterns are a form of seasonality.
Forecasts need back-testing or error measurement.
tasks.explanation: Operational forecasting should capture repeatable patterns, quantify error, and support scenarios rather than present one point estimate as certainty.
options: Model day-of-week seasonality using several comparable weeks, validate forecast error, and add scenario ranges before staffing decisions
Use only the single busiest Saturday as next month’s forecast
Assume every day has identical demand
Increase capacity without measuring forecast error

tasks.title: Design an Operational Cohort Comparison
tasks.context: Leadership wants to know whether a process change improved throughput over time.
tasks.goal: Define comparable operational cohorts without using patient identity or clinical characteristics.
tasks.prompt: How should the analyst structure the comparison?
tasks.expectedAnswer: Compare the same unit and comparable day-of-week periods before and after the process change, while tracking arrivals and capacity so mix changes are visible
hints: Keep the operating context comparable.
Day-of-week demand may differ.
Throughput can change because demand or capacity changed.
tasks.explanation: Operational cohorts should hold the process context as constant as practical and surface demand/capacity mix rather than attributing every change to the intervention.
options: Compare the same unit and comparable day-of-week periods before and after the process change, while tracking arrivals and capacity so mix changes are visible
Compare Emergency before the change with Outpatient after the change
Ignore arrival volume because throughput is all that matters
Use patient names to create cohorts

tasks.title: Write the Operations Executive Message
tasks.context: You found recurring weekend capacity gaps and higher Emergency waiting times in the synthetic operations data.
tasks.goal: Communicate an actionable but appropriately bounded insight.
tasks.expectedAnswer: Weekend demand exceeds planned capacity in the forecast and Emergency waits are higher on selected days; validate the pattern over more weeks and test scheduling or staffing scenarios before operational rollout
hints: State the evidence first.
Separate operations findings from clinical conclusions.
Recommend a controlled next step, not an unsupported certainty.
tasks.explanation: Strong executive communication is concise, decision-oriented, and explicit about uncertainty and scope.
options: Weekend demand exceeds planned capacity in the forecast and Emergency waits are higher on selected days; validate the pattern over more weeks and test scheduling or staffing scenarios before operational rollout
The data proves poor medical care
Immediately change treatment protocols
Hide the capacity gap until more data arrives
